I know many Americans like cushy, mushy steering and ride, and the sharp handling dynamics of a Tesla can hide the fact that you are making it mushy, but this car is capable of so much more!

text:
The Autopilot helped me eliminate Tesla from possible EV's I'll consider buying. I have a VW Alltrack with Adaptive Cruise Control very similar to Tesla cruise control, I also have Lane Assist.
I NEVER use Lane Assist for a few reasons namely the feedback thru the steering wheel it's like you're always fighting it, the car chooses where it wants to be in the lane and often it's too close to centerline like a 2 lane hwy (I prefer to drive over to the right in the lane, very often Lane Assist shuts down because it can't "see" the lines or there a gap in the road lines, Lane assist IMO is kind of unsafe (you cannot rely on it) so I never use it luckily unlike Tesla Autopilot I can shut off Lane Assist and still have Adaptive Cruise Control (which I Love) they're actually independent from each other  That's why I'd NEVER get a Tesla. Autopilot has merged 2 different functions and can not be separated not yet anyway maybe a software update could separate?
You didn't mention "PHANTOM BRAKING" (look it up) it's a major issue with Model 3 and Model Y and can be very dangerous the car can suddenly brake form any speed and come to a stop imagine that on a freeway...Phantom Braking happens when Autopilot is engaged! I can't help but wonder why Tesla integrated cruise control with autopilot...BIG mistake IMO. They lost me as a potential customer at least until they separate cruise control from lane assist so they're independent from each other.

author: @Resist4
text: You mean 240v, as there is no such thing as 220v for decades.  The mobile connector (not charger), is fine in a 240v outlet because if you always leave it plugged in, which is what people would do.  But any outlet will wear with plug in/out cycles, even your inside house 120v outlets.

author: @56ctconger
text:
Usual warning, do not attempt this if you are not knowledgeable about high voltage and current wiring.
You should use at the very least a high quality outlet. Some say you should not use aluminum wiring. This is because it oxidizes. Using a quality socket like even the midrange Hubble outlet with proper cable clamps tightened to the required spec, very tight, you should be fine. Just monitor the outlet temp for the first few days after charging for an hour. Then check once a month for a year and once every year after that.

With aluminum cables I believe if you select the lowest possible charging current setting consistent with your driving habits, likely about 30amps ( 3600watts), which will charge a battery depleted down to 35% in 10 hours, you should be fine as long as the clamps are clean and tight.
